title: The foreigner's prayer (1 Kings 8:41–43)
hook: Solomon asks that a stranger's prayer in the Temple be heard too

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon said no house could hold God. Your line was a place to turn toward. Today, in the same prayer, he makes room for someone outside his people.

Somebody arrives from far away. Different clothes, a different accent, maybe a different language. They've heard about this place and walked a long road to reach it. Now they stand in the courtyard among people who know the customs, and they don't. They pray anyway. Who is that prayer for? Will anyone listen? Solomon's dedication prayer, in the middle of asking for his own people, stops to answer exactly that.
screen: `SOMEBODY FROM FAR AWAY.` → `A LONG ROAD TO GET HERE.` → `WHO HEARS THEIR PRAYER?`

segments.voice: Solomon has prayed for Israel in defeat, in drought, in famine and plague. Then he turns to the foreigner, in Hebrew the nochri, who is not of Israel but comes out of a far country for the sake of God's name, having heard, the text says, of God's great name, strong hand and outstretched arm. When this stranger prays toward this house, Solomon asks, hear in heaven, and do according to all that the stranger calls to you for, so that all the peoples of the earth may know God's name. Later readers noticed a detail. For Israel, Solomon asks God to give each person according to their ways, since God knows the heart. For the foreigner, he asks God to do according to all they call for. The commentator Rashi reads that difference as care. Someone of Israel knows the relationship and can bear an answer of no. But a foreigner who is turned away might say, I came all this way to that house, and I wasn't heard. So, Rashi says, Solomon asked that the stranger be answered in full. Later, the prophet Isaiah speaks of God's house as a house of prayer for all peoples. And the Torah tells Israel to care for the stranger, because they were strangers in the land of Egypt. The house is built by one people, and it is open to another's voice.
screen: `NOCHRI: THE FOREIGNER.` · `DO ALL THAT THE STRANGER ASKS.` · `RASHI: SO NO ONE GOES HOME UNHEARD.` · `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLES.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind someone you don't know, a person you passed on the street, a new family down the block, someone far from home whose story you heard, and wonder what they might be asking for tonight: safety, work, a place to belong. If you pray, you can ask, in Solomon's spirit, that their prayer be heard; if you don't, just wish them well, plainly.
Nochri. The Hebrew word for a foreigner, the stranger from a far country Solomon asked God to hear fully. Today's word.
Your line: hear the stranger too. In Rashi's reading, the stranger shouldn't go home unheard. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read Solomon's prayer for the foreigner in the book of Kings alongside the Torah's command to care for the stranger, and commentators such as Rashi ask why the foreigner's prayer is to be answered in full.

chat.says: Did Solomon's Temple prayer include people who weren't Israelites?
options: Yes, he asked God to hear the foreigner from far away, and answer in full.
No, he prayed only for Israel, and strangers were kept out of the court.
Yes, but only foreigners already living inside Jerusalem's walls.
chat.meaning: Solomon asks God to hear the nochri, the foreigner, and do all they ask, so that all peoples may know God's name.

notes: All scripture here is paraphrased; no direct quotation.
